title: Introduce broken deployment
description: Project: Introduce broken deployment. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: A broken deployment is one of the most common causes of production incidents. It can arrive as a bad configuration, a missing migration, a port conflict, or a dependency version mismatch. This lesson covers how to detect, contain, and recover from a broken deployment, and how to build deployment pipelines that make rollbacks fast and reliable.

items: Application fails to start because a configuration value is missing or in the wrong format
Database migration applies but the new code expects a different schema, causing runtime errors
New dependency is incompatible with the target runtime or operating system
Health-check endpoint returns 503 because a downstream dependency is not ready yet
Feature flag accidentally toggles a half-finished feature for all users
Container image is built with the wrong environment variables, exposing secrets or disabling auth

terms.definition: A deployment package such as a container image or zip file that is built once and never modified in place.
Restoring a previous known-good version of an application after a bad deployment.
Running two identical environments and switching traffic from the old version to the new version.
Gradually shifting traffic to a new version while monitoring for errors before full rollout.
Managing and provisioning infrastructure through declarative configuration files rather than manual steps.

data.text: Rollback is not a failure of the deployment process; it is a feature of a healthy deployment process. Every deployment pipeline should include a tested rollback path. If you have never tested rolling back in production, you do not have a rollback strategy; you have a hope.

data.title: Health-check endpoint
data.content: An ASP.NET Core health check that verifies database and Redis connectivity before declaring the app ready:

items: Confirm the failure is deployment-related and not an underlying infrastructure issue
Roll back to the previous known-good version using your pipeline or platform
Verify health checks pass and error rate returns to baseline after rollback
Preserve the failed deployment artifact and logs for root cause analysis
Communicate status to stakeholders with a timeline and expected resolution

cards.title: Big-bang deployment
cards.description: All traffic switches to the new version at once.
cons: Long rollback time if something breaks

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.description: Two environments run in parallel; traffic switches atomically.
pros: Full environment for testing before switch

cards.title: Canary
cards.description: New version receives a small percentage of traffic first.
cons: Requires load balancer or service mesh support

data.title: Automate rollback triggers
data.text: Manual rollback decisions under incident pressure are slow and error-prone. Configure automated rollback when error rate exceeds a threshold for a sustained period. The cost of an unnecessary automatic rollback is lower than the cost of ten minutes of incident response.

items.question: How do I test rollback without risking production?
items.answer: Run rollback drills in staging using the same pipeline and artifact versions as production. Treat rollback testing as a deployment test case. If you cannot roll back in staging, you cannot roll back in production.

items.question: Should I fix forward or roll back?
items.answer: Roll back immediately to restore service, then fix forward with a hotfix or patch deployment. Fixing forward in production under pressure increases the risk of additional issues. Rolling back is the fastest path to user relief.

items.question: How do I handle database schema changes during rollback?
items.answer: Use backward-compatible migrations: add columns before deploying code that uses them, and remove columns only after the old version is fully decommissioned. Rolling back a schema change is far harder than rolling back application code.

data.title: Simulate a broken deployment
data.description: Deploy a new version that fails its health check. Practice rolling back using your deployment pipeline, then document the exact steps and timing.
steps: Introduce a deliberate failure in a staging environment
Trigger the deployment pipeline and verify the failure is detected
Execute the rollback procedure and time each step
Document the rollback runbook with exact commands and expected durations
Repeat until the rollback takes less than five minutes
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a tested, timed rollback procedure that any on-call engineer can execute without asking for help.

data.title: Summary
points: Broken deployments are common; design for fast detection and recovery
Automated health checks catch failures before users do
Rollback is a feature; test it regularly
Use backward-compatible migrations so schema changes do not block rollback
Keep failed artifacts and logs for post-incident analysis
data.takeaway: The measure of a deployment pipeline is not how fast it deploys; it is how fast it recovers when something goes wrong. Senior engineers invest in rollback automation because it pays back every time.
